articles.text: Authorities have arrested a suspect in the assault and residential robbery case that occurred last month on the 400 block of Scenic Avenue. The robbery occurred on March 24 as a man returned home around 12:25 a.m. to find his front door broken open and encountered two suspects inside. The man safely fled the residence and called 911. A woman inside the home was asleep at the time of the home invasion. She reported that two suspects entered her bedroom, demanded cash, and assaulted her when she was unable to comply. The two suspects ransacked the home of valuables before police could arrive. In an update on Tuesday, March 14, the Piedmont Police Department released a statement informing the public that an arrest had been made and the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office charged the individual with robbery. Officials did not release the suspect’s identity or say whether additional arrests are expected. The investigation has involved multiple agencies, including the Oakland Police Department, the Alameda County Sheriff’s Office, and the FBI’s Oakland field office, police said. “Public safety is a shared responsibility, and this case underscores how critical interagency collaboration is, particularly our strong working relationship with the Oakland Police Department,” said Police Chief Frederick Shavies. “I am grateful to the women and men of the Piedmont Police Department for their tireless efforts and commitment to keeping our community safe.” The investigation remains ongoing. The suspects were described as two Black men in their early 20s, approximately 5’10” and 6’0” tall, wearing gray and black hoodies. Anyone with information or who may have witnessed suspicious activity around this time is urged to contact the Piedmont Police Department at (510) 420-3000. articles.text: The fifth annual Piedmont Food Fest, a homegrown multicultural event, returns to Piedmont Park this Saturday, April 25 from 11am-4pm and will showcase some of the Bay Area’s most distinctive food trucks and stalls, breweries and wineries, and live performers. Together with the kid-favorite KidZone midway, guests will be treated to a full day of memorable entertainment — including a grand finale by the Cal Band to wrap up the event in style. As an-all volunteer run event, Piedmont Food Fest is the culmination of five months of planning involving over 100 volunteers and partners from Piedmont, Oakland, and the broader Bay Area. In pursuing its mission of celebrating the diversity of the Bay Area through food and music, Piedmont Food Fest has built a unique type of community centered around collectively enjoying new experiences together. As a result, Piedmont Food Fest brings together over 2000 visitors, 30 food and drink businesses, 10 local artists and performers, as well as many local sponsors, small businesses, and community groups to mix, mingle, and get to know one another. articles.text: If your ideal companion is social, communicative, and always close by, 9-year-old Nacho is ready to meet you. This outgoing orange boy is a true “shadow cat,” greeting you with cheerful meows, chatting back when you talk to him, and occasionally grooming your arm or leg to show his affection. He welcomes guests with confidence, and when he bonds deeply, you’ll know — he’ll follow you from room to room, curl up beside you in the mornings and evenings, and keep you company throughout the day. Nacho’s has a few medical conditions that are easily manageable: he takes a twice-daily inhaler for his asthma, with daily medications and a prescription diet to treat allergies, and gets regular check-ups to monitor his kidneys — all of which he handles well with positive reinforcement. articles.text: Cameron Wolfe and Valerie Matzger The reality of climate change has led the City of Piedmont and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation to collaborate on a major shift in plantings throughout the city to drought-tolerant California native plants. This replaces the water-thirsty non-native plants that have more traditionally been grown in Piedmont. The hope is that residents will see the options available to them to make the same shift in their own gardens. Several recent projects in public spaces illustrate that plants don’t have to drink copious amounts of water to be beautiful. These plant choices can also help to reverse the loss of insect populations, which generate the life support that keeps us, and all other living things, alive. The new Piedmont Aquatic Center dramatically illustrates this shift in plant choices. Plants are a major visual centerpiece of the new pool complex. The design by SWA Landscape Architects features drought-tolerant California native plants that support biodiversity by providing sustenance for pollinators, other beneficial insects, and birds. The existing large Coast live oak has been carefully preserved and another has been planted near the pool entrance. The wonderful fragrance of Winnifred Gilman sage surrounds the entrance path and the planting areas are filled with Howard McMinn Drought-tolerant Califronia native plants are seen in the foreground of this picture of the new Piedmont Aquatic Center. manzanita and the lower-growing Pacific Mist manzanita. The hedge along the Magnolia Avenue side is another very valuable wildlife supporter, the Holly-leaved cherry. A completely donor-funded organization, PBF made an early contribution to help kickstart the campaign in the amount of $25,000 and ultimately provided a total gift of $236,000. articles.text: Piedmont’s Annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration returns this Thursday, April 23, from 3:30 - 5:30 p.m., at Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. For this year’s event, the City is teaming up with East Bay Children & Nature, an Emeryvillebased organization dedicated to fostering stronger connections with nature in children. “We’re thrilled to be partnering with East Bay Children & Nature for this year’s Arbor & Earth Day celebration,” said Parks & Project Manager Nancy Kent. “The best part of this event every year is seeing the joy on children’s faces, and I think the collaboration this year is going to bring that to a whole new level. Beyond the immediate fun on the day itself, events like this help cultivate a lifelong love of nature and our planet.” The event will feature East Bay Children & Nature’s signature, “create-with-nature” stations that invite creativity and curiosity through play with natural materials. Two 20-minute sessions of nature-themed singalongs, starting at 4:15 p.m. and 5:10 p.m. Piedmont’s Public Works employees will be in attendance with the equipment they use in their daily work, including the Bay Area’s first fully electric closed-circuit TV sewer inspection van. Children will be able to climb up and sit in the cab of the Public Works trucks. There will be a raffle, and kids can enter to win a children’s book or toy related to Earth Day. The event will also feature plant giveaways. Attendees will have the opportunity to take home a California native plant for their gardens. Two professional arborists will be on hand to answer any questions about trees or plants that you may have. The annual event, which dates to 2007, celebrates the nearly 9,000 trees the Public Works Department maintains in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces – as well as the City’s commitment to environmental stewardship. The Arbor Day celebration will also include am announcement of the 2026 Piedmont Heritage Trees. Nominators of selected trees will be recognized at the event and receive a Piedmont Heritage Tree lapel pin. The Heritage Tree program, now in its eighth year, aims to raise awareness of and appreciation for Piedmont’s diverse urban forest. Heritage Trees are nominated by community members and selected by the Park Commission. articles.text: Piedmont’s Shell Station at 29 Wildwood Avenue has been in limbo ever since a city-approved plan for an EV charging hub was upended due to state laws that limit local control over EV charging station permits. Now the station’s development is in the hands of the state and the Alameda County Department of Environmental Health (ACEHD). According to ACEHD, Previous environmental investigations have identified elevated concentrations of volatile organic compounds and petroleum hydrocarbons in soil, groundwater, and soil vapor (the air between soil particles) at the site. Due to these findings, the department has required Shell to conduct both on‑site and off‑site environmental assessments at 29 Wildwood Avenue, including work under a Voluntary Remedial Action Agreement and a detailed subsurface investigation. Under this agreement, Shell voluntarily agrees to investigate and clean up environmental contamination. This work includes collecting soil, soil vapor, and groundwater samples from 29 Wildwood and two neighboring off-site residential properties. The investigations will be performed to evaluate if these contaminants have migrated beyond the site, and to verify that conditions are protective of site utility workers and adjacent residents. The latest on-site and off-site environmental investigation was conducted on March 6. Once the investigation is complete, Shell will work with ACEHD to develop and review an appropriate Remedial Action Plan. The plan will address contamination and ensure long-term protection of public health and the environment. According to a representative from Shell, the timing and feasibility of redevelopment will depend on the extent of remediation required, regulatory approvals, and other potential factors such as weather and access to adjacent properties. Because these steps are still in progress, Shell does not yet have a confirmed construction timeline for the charging station. Should residents have any questions or concerns, contact Tracy Craig at (510) 334-4866 (24/7). Project details can be found at: https://geotracker.waterboards.ca.gov and searching for the address 29 Wildwood Avenue, Piedmont. articles.text: Children’s Fairyland is celebrating the magic of spring with an event especially designed for the forever young at heart. It will take place on Friday, April 24 from 6-10 p.m. The immersive adults-only Alice in Wonderland-themed party will feature Wonderland mischief and theatrical surprises, a proper tea party, local food trucks, sweet Wonderland-inspired treats, a DJ with a black light dance floor, and surprise activations throughout the park. Guests can explore the iconic park, sip on curated cocktails, mocktails, beer, wine, and other beverages. Guests can feel free to express themselves with imaginative attire, whimsical accessories, or elaborate outfits. Costumes are highly encouraged, but not required. Mad Tea Party is centered around a proper tea party at the park’s famous Jack and Jill Hill. A live DJ atop the hill will help turn the space into a whimsical world of tea, beats, and Wonderland treats. Guests can enjoy a cup of tea, themed sweets, and party favors while cabaret performers bring Alice in Wonderland to life with meandering vignettes and circus surprises. The Red Queen makes cameos throughout the evening and other performers roam the park creating wandering theatrical mischief for all to enjoy. Fairyland is a playground for the inner child of every grownup in attendance. Guests are invited to hop aboard the Jolly Trolly for delightful evening rides, play inside the Alice in Wonderland tunnel and maze, and explore other storybook sets like the Old West Junction and many more. With 10 acres of lush gardens, attractions, water features, and whimsical structures, there is something magical to discover with every corner turned. This year’s Mad Tea Party welcomes back crowd favorite DJ heyLove who blends jazz, R&B, hip-hop, house, and global rhythms into soulful, genre-defying sets. She’ll be spinning choice cuts with a black light dance floor where guests can enjoy a unique experience in the Merry Meadow under the Oakland stars in neon colored revelry. A stanchioned top of the Dragon Slide becomes an exclusive VIP lounge for a select group of people who want to enjoy an elevated experience featuring champagne, bottle service, and gorgeous photo ops. While this year’s Gilded Chrysalis Experience is completely sold out, this tier ticketing option is new and is set to become a consistent feature of the annual event. Fairyland’s Gift Shop will be open for the event where guests can find an array of adults-only merchandise rolled out for the evening and can also purchase their own copy of Fairyland’s signature piece of magical merch: the Magic Key. articles.text: Dear PUSD Families & Staff: What a remarkable spring it has been, and it’s hard to believe we are closing in on the end of the school year. Our students had the rare experience of traveling to China, Spain, and France, travels that will likely shape their understanding of the world for years to come. A heartfelt thank you to our students and families for your enthusiasm, flexibility, and trust, and to all of our dedicated teachers and administrators who initiated and chaperoned these trips. Organizing international travel for groups of students requires extensive preparation, meticulous planning, and an enormous personal commitment, and we are deeply grateful for your leadership and care. Having served as one of the chaperones on the China trip, I can say with complete sincerity that it was one of the best trips of my life. Our students experienced an incredible range of cultural, historical, and modern wonders: walking the Great Wall, taking in the breathtaking Longji Terraced Rice Fields, cruising the Lijiang River, admiring the Temple of Heaven, the Forbidden City, and Tiananmen Square in Beijing, touring factories and robotics facilities in Tangshan, and visiting two local schools where students connected with their Chinese peers. A very special thank you is owed to XinJia Xia (Xia laoshi) for her extraordinary work organizing this journey across multiple cities, hotels, schools, and cultural experiences. Her expertise, tireless effort, and joy made this trip the remarkable success it was. It gave us the chance to spend real, uninterrupted time together doing things we all enjoy, including camping, hiking, and even launching rockets on the beach. Those are the moments that stay with you. It’s been just as meaningful to watch the other kids in the troop grow into confident, capable young adults, and to know we had a small part in that along the way. articles.text: After three years on the Public Safety Committee, Liz Lummis O’Neil’s term has ended. She spent years emphasizing the importance of community involvement and fire safety. Liz valued the opportunity to volunteer, learn, and connect with fellow Piedmont residents, viewing it as a way to contribute positively to the community. Liz moved to Piedmont in 2016 and decided to be a part of the tight-knit community by volunteering. After attending a random City Council meeting, Liz had the opportunity to speak with the Fire Chief at the time. This led to her neighborhood having a fire safety meeting. Liz realized the idea of fire safety had been on her mind for a while, and she finally found the avenue to spread awareness. “When I came to California, way back when, in 1992, it was just after the firestorm in Upper Rockridge. So Fire Safety has always been on the top of my mind. To get to join the Piedmont Public Safety Committee meant a lot. It wasn’t sitting and hoping nothing happens, but rather being informed and taking action,” said O’Neil. After joining the Public Safety Liz O’Neil shakes hands with Piedmont Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen after receiving a volunteer award for her time with the Public Safety Committee. Committee in 2023, Liz felt her role was to act as a sounding board and keep her neighborhood informed. “I wanted to be the voice of my neighborhood. If something ever came up, I would be good at voicing our perspective and keeping our neighborhood informed,” O’Neil said. Liz reflected on her term on the Public Safety Committee, stating the importance of community involvement and informing people about wildfire safety. “One of my takeaways was that Piedmont residents like to take action and make things happen. A recent project I worked on was having Captain Callahan and some of his crew come over from the fire department to give an in-depth fire safety meeting for homes, and then did individual walk-throughs of each of the attending group’s homes,” Liz continued. Friday, April 17 was a momentous occasion for the Piedmont High swimming team, debuting at the Piedmont Pool against Castro Valley. It was the first time the Highlanders hosted a meet since 2019. articles.text: Piedmont fell to O’Dowd in a pair of one-run games. Piedmont’s baseball team had a tightly contested series with rival Bishop O’Dowd losing a pair of one-run ball games. The Highlanders hosted the Dragons on Wednesday, April 15 and lost 3-2 in a heated 11-inning game. They followed up with a close 1-0 loss at O’Dowd two days later on Friday, April 17. Piedmont had to play both games without its star hitter, Diego Delventhal. “He’s a quality at bat, he’ll still be a couple of weeks, but no one is feeling sorry for us,” coach Eric Olson said. PHS held a 2-1 lead in Wednesday’s game following the bottom of the sixth, but the Dragons tied things up in the top of the seventh and scored the game-winner in the top of the 11th. In Friday’s game, Bishop O’Dowd logged the games only hit. “A lot of guys stepped up their game. We had some good pitching to prolong the game and give us a chance. The defense was solid, which is what we’re looking for. We were just one hit away from getting runs,” Olson said. The Highlanders hold a 6-10-2 (W-L-T) record with just six games left in its regular season. Coming up are two-game series with Alameda, Berkeley, and Encinal. Staff Photos 3-2 loss to O’Dowd in extra innings O’Dowd went up 1-0 in the top of the second, while Piedmont answered with two runs in the bottom of the sixth. The Dragons tied things up in the top of the seventh, and scored once more in the top of the 11th. In the bottom of the sixth, Enzo Ong led off with a walk, followed by Lucas Delventhal singling on a bunt. Jonah Cha-Foster followed up with a bunt of his own, and was ruled safe at first after colliding with the first-baseman in his way. That allowed Ong to score. Jack Meyjes then grounded out to the shortstop, allowing Delventhal to score. However, that was all Piedmont could muster. PHS had a chance to win the game in the bottom of the seventh after Aiden Bell and Max Fujimoto walked, followed by George Bishop singling on a bunt to load the bases. But after that, Massimo Mittone grounded out, a squeeze bunt by Ong failed, and Delventhal popped out. O’Dowd scored the game-winner with two outs, where Marco Cecchin stole third and then scored when Delventhal came narrowly short of throwing out Charlie Sellman to end the inning on a hard hit ground ball. Freshman Ben Sorensen had a productive outing against BOD, throwing six innings and four strikeouts in Wednesday’s no decision. George Bishop threw 4.2 innings in Wednesday’s game, striking out five.

articles.text: Pianist Yuja Wang will perform at Davies Symphony Hall on April 26. World-renowned pianist Yuja Wang performs with the Mahler Chamber Orchestra at Davies Symphony Hall this Sunday, April 26. Wang, a Chinese-born classical pianist from Beijing, made her San Francisco Symphony debut in 2006 and toured Asia with the company and its former conductor Michael Tilson Thomas in November 2012. She has since become a recurring guest pianist at Davies Symphony Hall and has performed with the Berlin Philharmonic, Oslo Philharmonic, Toronto Symphony Orchestra and more. Wang is celebrated for both her stage presence and musical skills, and returns to San Francisco next month to direct a program of 20th-century favorites by Prokofiev with the Mahler Chamber Orchestra. The program included Alexander Tsfasman’s Suite for Piano and Orchestra (Jazz Suite). The Mahler Chamber Orchestra is a professional touring chamber orchestra founded by Claudio Abbado and former members of the Gustav Mahler Youth Orchestra in 1997. The orchestra consists of 45 musicians from 20 nations and performs more than 60 concerts a year worldwide. Matthew Truscott serves as concertmaster and leader for the evening concert. Performance begins at 7:30 p.m. Visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2025-26/ YUJA-WANG-MCO to purchase tickets, or call the San Francisco Symphony box office at (415) 864-6000.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony concludes its 2026 Chamber Series at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on May 31 with a curated program highlighting contemporary voices and classical masterworks, held The concert, titled “I, Too, Sing America,” is curated by James Parrish Smith, featuring works by Brian Raphael Nabors, Anna Clyne and Antonín Dvořák. Smith currently serves as the Organist and Director of Music at the First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley. He previously served as Director of Music and Organist at the Historic Third Baptist Church of San Francisco and was the Founding Director of the Bridge to Arts and Music Program in association with the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. “This season represents an exciting new chapter for Berkeley Symphony,” said Berkeley Symphony Executive Director Marion Atherton. “We’re thrilled to welcome some of today’s most compelling conductors, each bringing their unique artistic vision to our stage.” This season “shines a light on stirring masterpieces from the James Parrish Smith classical canon alongside groundbreaking contemporary works,” Atherton added. “From Dvorák’s lyrical Eighth Symphony to Shostakovich’s spirited Ninth and Haydn’s vivid ‘Military’ Symphony, we’re exploring rich musical territory beyond the standard repertoire while showcasing the versatility and excellence of our orchestra.” The 2025/26 season also marks the conclusion of Music Director Joseph Young’s successful six-year tenure. Young first guest-conducted the Berkeley Symphony in 2019 as an emergency substitute conductor. Based on that concert, in April 2019, the Berkeley Symphony announced the appointment of Young as its next music director, marking his first major directorship in symphonic music. Chamber Series subscriptions are $120 and available through the symphony’s box office and website. Individual tickets and subscriptions may be purchased by calling the box office at (510) 841-2800 or visiting berkeleysymphony.org.

articles.text: The Gardens of Golden Gate Park (GGGP), the nonprofit organization that operates the Conservatory of Flowers, Japanese Tea Garden, and San Francisco Botanical Garden, hosts its annual fundraising gala on Saturday, May 9. The annual benefit supports programming, services and events hosted by the GGGP. Proceeds from the gala provide support to sustain the gardens’ diverse living collections and allow GGGP to provide education resources for Bay Area families year-round. This year’s gala honors Ruth and Ken Wilcox, longtime ambassadors and friends to the gardens, and welcomes award-winning author and contributing New York Times writer Margaret Renkl as guest speaker. Renkl is the author of Late Migrations: A Natural History of Love and Loss and Graceland and Notes on Hope and Heartache from the American South. Her most recent work, The Comfort of Crows: A Backyard Year solidifies her reputation as “one of the most thoughtful voices in contemporary American nature writing.” Her children’s book, The Weedy Garden, explores the vibrant ecosystem of a backyard gardener. Weedy Garden will be released next month. Tiered sponsorship levels are now available for purchase online. Visit https://gggp.org/gala/ to purchase tickets.

articles.text: A major retrospective of artist Maren Hassinger opens June 6 at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA), offering a wide-ranging look at her five-decade career. Titled Maren Hassinger: Living Moving Growing, the exhibition will be on view from June 6 through November 29. Organized as the most comprehensive survey of Hassinger’s work to date, the show will include more than twenty works spanning the 1970s to the present, alongside newly created installations and performances developed in collaboration with the artist. T he ex h ibit ion br i ngs together sculpture, installation, video, and performance, reflecting Hassinger’s interdisciplinary approach. Known for working with both industrial and impermanent materials, she has explored themes of movement, environment, and human connection throughout her career. Because many of her works are ephemeral, several pieces will be recreated specifically for this presentation. Among the featured works are Love (2008), a site-specific installation made from inflated pink plastic bags containing handwritten notes, and Beach (1980), a floor installation composed of plaster and wooden dowels. Additional sculptures incorporating freshly harvested tree branches will be produced in partnership with the University of California Botanical Garden. A central component of the exhibition will be public participation. On opening day, visitors will be invited to join Hassinger in creating a new installation titled Wrenching News by twisting and knotting newspapers in a workshop led by the artist. The piece will evolve over time through monthly workshops facilitated by Berkeley-based artist Julia Goodman. Hassinger will also return to Berkeley on September 20 to restage Pink Trash, a performance she has presented only twice since its debut in 1982. The work will involve six UC Berkeley undergraduates collaborating with the artist to scatter and transform discarded litter, which will be repainted pink. The performance will take place on the university’s Crescent Lawn. In addition to artworks, the exhibition will include archival photographs and videos, including previously unpublished images documenting early works that no longer exist. The retrospective is co-curated by Margot Norton, Chief Curator, and Anthony Graham, Senior Curator, with Curatorial Assistant Omar Jason Farah. An accompanying catalogue featuring new scholarship and interviews will be published in conjunction with the exhibition. “Maren Hassinger’s practice has been of great influence for generations of artists–from her early collaborative performances and experimental installations with Studio Z and JAM to her direct impact over decades as a teacher, and through her monumental sculptural installations in major museum collections across the United States,” said Norton. “We are thrilled to finally bring her artworks and their stories from across her career together through our exhibition, and to showcase Hassinger’s profound contributions to contemporary art.” “ For d e c a d e s , M a r e n Hassinger has created sculptures and installations that transcend disciplinary boundaries, transforming industrial and mass-produced materials into evocative abstractions,” said Graham. “This exhibition showcases how these innovative works have drawn attention to subtle movements and forms of our everyday lives, connecting us to one another and to the world around us.” “Maren Hassinger’s work invites us to reflect on the beauty and complexity of human connection—through movement, material, and shared experience. Presenting this landmark retrospective at BAMPFA underscores our commitment to amplifying artists whose practices challenge conventions and inspire collective engagement across generations,” said BAMPFA Executive Director Julie Rodrigues Widholm. More information about this and other public programs will be announced this summer at bampfa.org. Maren Hassinger

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), California’s oldest independent youth orchestra, presents the America 250 Festival, a celebration of American Music on Saturday, May 2 at 7:00 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. The special festival concert commemorates the 250th anniversary of the United States with an evening of chamber and orchestral works by American composers spanning more than a century of musical history. The concert also serves as YPSO’s annual Spring Concert as the third concert in its 2025–26 subscription series. As part of nationwide celebrations of America’s 250th anniversary the festival explores the musical traditions that have shaped the American orchestral landscape while highlighting the role of young musicians in carrying that legacy forward. Presented in an expanded festival format, the event features chamber music performed by YPSO musicians, followed by a full orchestral program. The festival highlights the diversity and creativity of American composers, from iconic figures such as Aaron Copland and Leonard Bernstein to influential contemporary voices including Jessie Montgomery, George Walker, and Kenji Bunch. The first half of the festival showcases chamber music performed by YPSO musicians in different ensembles, including strings, brass, winds, and percussion. These smaller ensembles offer audiences an intimate musical experience while allowing students to collaborate closely and explore a wide range of styles and traditions. “Chamber music encompasses important musical techniques of listening, blending, and playing together like no other musical genre,” said Julie Kim, YPSO’s Chamber Music Director. “At the America 250 Festival, we will feature several combinations of ensembles to showcase American composers at their best.” The second half of the program brings the full orchestra to the stage with a selection of works that highlight the breadth and evolution of American orchestral music across generations. “This America 250 Festival program represents a range of American voices in classical music, both chamber and symphonic, from the 20th and 21st centuries,” said YPSO Music Director David Ramadanoff. This project is supported in part by a grant from the National Endowment for the Arts. Tickets are $20 and students are free (registration is required). If someone died before Mountain View was established in 1863, they were typically buried at the Catholic Cemetery. It was not until 1968 that the Catholic Church permitted its members to be buried at Mountain View. In 1864, the Jewish community purchased two acres from Mountain View on its northern edge, creating a dedicated burial area. Evanosky added that the name “Mountain View” is common among cemeteries nationwide, with hundreds sharing it. The walk combined history, storytelling, and a chance to reflect on the community’s past, fitting for a group that has spent eight years exploring Piedmont and its surroundings on foot. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. Those interested should go to https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or call (510) 420-3070 for more information.

articles.text: High in the rugged hills of the Santa Cruz Mountains, Ridge Vineyards stands as one of California’s most respected and historically significant wineries. Known for its commitment to traditional winemaking and sitedriven wines, Ridge has built a reputation over more than six decades as a producer of some of America’s finest Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah and Zinfandel. Though the modern winery was established in 1962, Ridge’s roots stretch back much further. The Monte Bello estate, its flagship vineyard, was first planted in 1885 by Italian doctor Osea Perrone, who recognized the potential of the limestone-rich soils and high elevation. The site produced its first wine in 1892 before falling into decline after Prohibition. It was not until a group of Stanford Research Institute engineers purchased and revived the property in the late 1950s that Ridge Vineyards was reborn. From the beginning, Ridge embraced a philosophy that set it apart. The winery has long championed single-vineyard wines, believing that the finest expressions of wine come from specific sites where soil, climate, and grape variety align. This approach is exemplified in its flagship Monte Bello, a Cabernet Sauvignon-based blend that has become one of California’s most iconic wines. Ridge’s rise to international prominence came in 1976, when its 1971 Monte Bello placed fifth in the historic Judgment of Paris, a blind tasting. The result shocked the wine world by demonstrating that California wines could rival those of France. In a 30th anniversary re-tasting, Monte Bello was ranked number one, cementing its legacy as a world-class wine. Equally important to Ridge’s identity is its dedication to “pre-industrial” winemaking – a philosophy popularized by longtime winemaker Paul Draper. This approach emphasizes minimal intervention, native yeast fermentation, and transparency, including listing ingredients on labels. Long before such practices became fashionable, Ridge was quietly producing wines that reflected both authenticity and restraint. Today, Ridge operates two primary facilities: the Monte Bello estate in the Santa Cruz Mountains and Lytton Springs in Sonoma County’s Dry Creek Valley. While Monte Bello is synonymous with structured, age-worthy Cabernet blends, Lytton Springs is celebrated for its expressive Zinfandel-based wines. Together, they showcase Ridge’s mastery of both Bordeaux and California heritage varietals. Despite changes in ownership – most notably its acquisition by Japan’s Otsuka Pharmaceutical in 1986 – Ridge has remained remarkably consistent in its philosophy and style. Its wines continue to earn critical acclaim, with Monte Bello frequently cited among the greatest Cabernet Sauvignons produced in the United States. In an industry often driven by trends, Ridge Vineyards has succeeded by staying true to its principles. Its enduring focus on terroir, transparency, and tradition ensures that it remains not only a cornerstone of California wine history but also a benchmark for its future. Deep garnet-purple in color, it charges out of the glass with exuberant black cherry, plum and blueberry notions with touches of dark chocolate, cloves and violets. Full-bodied yet balanced, the palate is decadently fruited with black and blue berry flavors framed by firm yet plush tannins and seamless freshness, finishing with wonderfully long-lasting, baking spice nuances. Cabernet just doesn’t get any better than this. • 2023 Ridge Cabernet Sauvignon Estate This is the baby brother to the Montebello but is an outstanding wine in its own right. Sourced in the Santa Cruz Mountain AVA it offers stony notes intermixed with cassis and gravel along with a striking minerality, rich deep cassis fruit, well-concealed and integrated American oak, and a long, structured finish. This wine will develop even more complexity with time in the cellar and will last for two decades.

articles.text: After a year of intentional writing, and a lifetime of learning, I am honored to introduce my newest book, Mindset In Motion™: Activate Purpose, Passion, and Peak Performance. Living and working in the Piedmont and East Bay community, I’ve had the privilege of connecting with individuals and families at every stage of life, first-time buyers, growing families, entrepreneurs, and those thoughtfully transitioning into their next chapter. These conversations, often centered around home and lifestyle, reveal something deeper: a universal desire for growth, clarity, and purpose. This book was born from those moments. It is written for individuals at every age and stage, those beginning anew, navigating change, or stepping into what’s next. While circumstances may differ, the desire to move forward with intention is something we all share. I was reminded of this while working with a client preparing to leave a longtime family home. What began as a real estate decision quickly became a reflection on identity, memories, and possibility. The challenge wasn’t just logistical, it was emotional. It required mindset, trust, and ultimately, action. That experience reinforced what I’ve seen time and again: people rarely lack opportunity. More often, they lack momentum. Mindset In Motion™ was created to address that gap. At its core, the book bridges inspiration with aligned action. It invites readers to move beyond intention and into execution, to activate purpose, sustain passion, and pursue peak performance in a meaningful and attainable way. The foundation is the Mindset In Motion Method™, a five-step framework: Goal, Believe, Internalize, Share, and Activate. Clarity of goals establishes direction. Belief fosters possibility. Internalization transforms identity. Sharing cultivates connection. And activation—consistent, intentional action—drives results. This method is designed to support anyone navigating life’s transitions, whether overcoming adversity or addiction, stepping into an empty nest, building a company or personal brand, or simply ready to conquer a longheld goal and move forward with clarity and confidence. What distinguishes Mindset In Motion™ is its practicality. Each chapter includes GOALS, ACTION, and CON NECT prompts, encouraging readers to apply the principles in real time and create forward momentum. This reflects a philosophy I’ve come to embrace: insight alone does not create change. It is the Debbi DiMaggio’s latest book Debbi DiMaggio is a Piedmont resident, real estate advisor, coach & author combination of mindset and movement that leads to meaningful progress. In a community like ours, where lifestyle, design, and quality of life are deeply valued, there is also an opportunity to pause and ask: How are we growing? Where are we going next? And what is required to get there? Because ultimately, growth is not defined by age or circumstance, but by the willingness to take the next step. As I share Mindset In Motion™ with the Piedmont and East Bay community, my hope is that it serves as both a guide and a catalyst, supporting individuals in moving forward with clarity, confidence, and purpose. Mindset In Motion™: Activate Purpose, Passion, and Peak Performance is now available on Amazon. To learn more, visit www.MindsetInMotionBook. com. — Debbi DiMaggio Piedmont Resident, Real Estate Advisor, Coach & Author GOOD THROUGH MAY 2026 GOOD THROUGH MAY 2026 GOOD THROUGH MAY 2026 GOOD THROUGH MAY 2026

articles.text: Marking Piedmont Scout Council’s rich history, a capacity crowd attended the 105th annual Recognition Dinner at the Guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church on April 16. “Scouting is a journey we learn every step of the way. We get involved because of our kids, we stay involved because we see the power of the program,” said Piedmont Scouting President Glyn Burge. “I think sometimes we need to pause and ask ourselves, ‘Why are we doing this?’ Perhaps one answer is that scouting is more important than ever in helping our youth develop into responsible citizens and community members. I believe firmly in the scouting program and the benefits it offers all our youth.” Burge discussed Scouting America’s current turmoil with the federal government. The Pentagon threatens to cut support for the Scouts unless the organization reverts to “core values” and realigns itself with service to “God and country”. “Unfortunately, our federal government doesn’t see it that way. I hope you will join me in continuing to support the scouting programs, both in Piedmont and beyond. It’s a lot to be under attack from a government that doesn’t seem to understand what we’re trying to do,” said Burge. Paul Jahn is this year’s honoree for the Silver Beaver recognition, the highest recognition a council can give a volunteer. 2025’s Silver Beaver recipient Jim Riley presented the award to Jahn, praising him for his excelAfter the dinner, all Silver Beaver honorees gathered for a group photo. Paul Jahn was presented with the 2026 Silver Beaver award by 2025’s Silver Beaver Jim Riley. The crowd is settling in, ready for the dinner to start. NESA Outstanding Eagle Scout Award presented to Bryan Cantrill and Todd Reynolds. Kevin Fischer and Ken Li present the William Peterson Youth Leadership Award to Scouts Evan Friedman and Stephanie Lee. District Award of Merit given to Brian Kelleher and Dante Rodriguez. The crowd is cheering for President Glyn Burge’s passionate ending statement. lent work with the Scouts. Jahn has been an executive board member for the past 8 years. He is currently serving as Past President and Nominating Committee Chairman. He was a council president from 2023-2025 and has been an Assistant Scout Master for Troop 1 for the past 8 years. It is a point of pride for Jahn that a quarter of Piedmont youth have similar formative experiences in the Scouting program. Jahn notes this is possible because of “the incredible support of our community for the Scouting movement and the many wonderful, dedicated volunteers putting their heart and soul into working with our kids.” Another recognition of note was the NESA Outstanding Eagle Scout Award (NOESA), presented to two honorees, Bryan Cantrill and Todd Reynolds. The award is presented to Eagle Scouts who demonstrate remarkable achievements well beyond their Scouting endeavors by excelling in their careers/vocations at local, regional, or national levels. Cantrill has excelled in the computer science field as a software engineer. He’s a co-founder and CTO of Oxide Computer Company, and before Oxide, he spent nine years at Joyent, a software and services company. Reynolds is the Water Treatment Practice Leader at Kennedy Jenks, bringing extensive expertise in water treatment and engineering solutions, supported by a Master of Arts from the University of California, Berkeley. Before joining Kennedy Jenks, Reynolds served as a Nuclear Submarine Officer in the United States Navy. At the dinner, the council also recognized other volunteers who have made a significant difference in the community. Pack 5: Scott Zengel Pack 6: Katie Larson

articles.text: In late 2022, Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted and Associate Pastor Don Ashburn introduced Life Groups to Piedmont Community Church. The idea of a Life Group is to create a safe place where people can connect with each other and bring honest questions about faith and life. They create a kind of “neighborhood within a community” in a time when people feel isolated and fearful and need other people whom we trust to help us and to support us and our families as we navigate new waters, life challenges and grow spiritually. The program has been a huge success. Now, in 2026, over 70 members of the congregation are participating in a Life Group. Many new members join a Life Group immediately to get acquainted and become integrated into the life of the Church. Long-time members welcome the opportunity to nurture cherished friendships and build new ones. A Life Group consists of 8-10 people who meet weekly for six weeks to discuss the Sunday sermon and the scripture on which it is based. A sermon summary and set of questions to consider is available before the meeting and fuels the discussion that is led by a group leader. Life Group sessions happen four times a year. Long-time members welcome the opportunity to nurture cherished friendships and build new ones. pages.text: Piedmont Council Scouting programs are designed to help youth build character, fitness, citizenship, and leadership skills. The life lessons learned in Scouting form a foundation for youth to embrace opportunity and overcome obstacles in life. In Scouting, youth learn to do things themselves and take an active role in leading their programs. Further, Scouting programs are inclusive and collaborative. Today’s youth are our future citizens, parents, and leaders. We help youth grow into adults who make ethical choices, and who have the skills to carry those choices out. PROGRAM SUPPORT Council activities provided support to unit programs throughout the year, including: • A Camporee adventure at Camp Tamarancho that pulled Scouts BSA troops together for a skills competition in the outdoors. • The Highlander Hiker Series also included a clean up at Sausal Creek, Scouting for Food, an archery day, and a Bike Fest at Havens Elementary School. • Order of the Arrow – the honor society for Scouts BSA – provided service at Camp Augusta through two inductions in spring and fall, and supported the Cub Scout Overnighter. Some examples of Eagle projects include a STEAM wall for Thornhill Elementary School, an obstacle course for Piedmont elementary schools, octagonal benches, and an online Piedmont Football historical archive. Outside of Eagle projects, Scouts BSA troops helped clean Sausal Creek, picked up 8,500 pounds of food for the Alameda County Community Food Bank, and supported camps in and out of Scouting. Estimated service to the community through these projects is more than 2,000 hours. Piedmont Community Service Crew youth spend many hours each month planning and cooking meals for the food insecure. A big project this year was planning, organizing, constructing, and funding an office for the Richmond Tiny House Village. The crew also spent 6 days building tiny houses in Oregon and took an international trip to Ethiopia. In total, the Venturers of PCSC logged 2,806 service hours. Adventure Highlight: Northern Tier High Adventure Trek Northern Tier is the premier high adventure experience for wilderness canoeing. A Council contingent of two crews ventured out from the Atikokan, Ontario base into the Quetico. This is a gorgeous and pure wilderness, with minimal traces of human travel. Each of the crews completed a 7-day canoe trek through the wilderness. “The Scouts and adults were able to experience another Crew 1 country, and this base is by far the most remote,” said Lisa Gros, one of the trip leaders. “The Quetico Provincial Park is immaculately maintained. You really get a sense of the vastness and amazing gift of being there and seeing it. As an adult, it is a gift to see the tremendous growth and resiliency in the Scouts. They truly go through a transformational process.” Trip highlights: Crew 2 • Day 2: Fern Lake was beautiful and narrow at the top, with shale-like formations. It was brutal portage on the Pickeral River. On some maps, the portage shows as two different portages, but today they form one long portage. The toughest part is not the heavy gear – it is the slippery rocks, trip hazards, mud, and the heavy and cumbersome gear, especially the canoes. • Day 6: It was a fast and efficient paddle to Beaverhouse Lake. We had one portage, which was easy and forgettable. But as we got back into the water, there was a little rapid to navigate. We all made it down the rougher water easily, though Rafi and Connor gave us a little scare with their wobble.” Crew 1 did lots of fishing (34 fish total caught!), completed portages and two merit badges, and weathered several storms.
